title: Type Qualifiers & Specifiers
relevance: Interviewers probe const-correctness, volatile, and restrict to test whether candidates understand compiler contracts, UB, and when optimizers may legally break naive code.

phases.goal: Establish that type qualifiers/specifiers change the contract with the compiler, not how data is fundamentally represented.

must_hit.point: Type qualifiers and specifiers are metadata on C declarations that dictate what the compiler may and may not do when optimizing, rather than typically changing memory representation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says they alter the contract with the compiler/optimizer, not the fundamental layout of the data.

must_hit.point: const declares that an object's value will not be modified after initialization and underpins const-correctness: functions advertise whether they modify data passed to them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions post-init immutability and functions promising read-only access (e.g. strlen taking const char *).

must_hit.point: A pointer-to-const parameter is a binding promise not to write through that pointer; attempting to write yields a compile error and lets callers pass read-only data safely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites strlen/strcpy-style contracts: read src, never mutate it through the const-qualified pointer.

probes: What do type qualifiers actually change in a C program, and what does const promise about a function parameter?

hints.1: Think about what the compiler is allowed to assume, not about bits in memory.
hints.2: Separate representation of the object from the contract about mutation after initialization.
hints.3: const means no modification after init; a const-qualified pointees parameter means the callee will not write through that pointer.

phases.goal: Pin down const placement on pointers, volatile's effect on loads/stores, and restrict's anti-aliasing promise.

must_hit.point: const position relative to * yields four cases: int *p (both mutable); const int *p / int const *p (data immutable through p, pointer movable); int * const p (pointer fixed, data mutable); const int * const p (neither address nor data changeable through p).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the four combinations and reads declarations with the right-left rule.

must_hit.point: volatile tells the compiler an object can change outside known control flow: do not cache it in registers, do not elide reads/writes, and respect the abstract-machine sequence of accesses as physical reads/writes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains register caching of loop reads vs forced fresh memory access each iteration for volatile.

must_hit.point: restrict (C99) promises that for the pointer's lifetime, if the pointed-to object is modified, all accesses go through that restrict pointer (or pointers derived from it)—i.e. no aliasing via other paths.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the non-aliasing promise and contrasts memcpy (restrict) with memmove (no such promise).

must_hit.point: Global or static const objects are typically placed in a read-only segment (often .rodata in ELF); casting away const and modifying an object originally defined as const is undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions .rodata/read-only placement and UB/segfault risk if const is cast away and written.

probes: Explain the difference between const int *p and int * const p, then what volatile and restrict each force the compiler to assume.

hints.1: Read from the identifier outward: where const sits relative to * matters.
hints.2: Map three ideas: what may mutate (const), what must hit memory every time (volatile), and whether two pointers may overlap (restrict).
hints.3: const int * = movable pointer, immutable data through it; int * const = fixed pointer; volatile = every abstract read/write is a real access; restrict = sole access path if the object is modified.

phases.goal: Contrast tools that look similar—volatile vs _Atomic, and restricted vs unrestricted copy—and when const combines with volatile.

must_hit.point: volatile provides visibility against compiler caching for hardware/ISRs but is not atomic and not a memory barrier; _Atomic (C11) provides atomicity and memory ordering for OS threads.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says use volatile for hardware/interrupts; use _Atomic or mutexes for threads—not volatile alone.

must_hit.point: memcpy uses restrict and may vectorize assuming non-overlapping buffers; memmove makes no restrict promise, is safe for overlapping memory, but may be slower.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the overlap-safety vs optimization tradeoff between memcpy and memmove.

must_hit.point: const volatile is coherent for a read-only hardware register: volatile forces re-reads because hardware changes it; const forbids the C program from writing it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a status/timer register example that hardware updates but software must only read.

probes: Is volatile enough to share data between threads? How does that compare to _Atomic, and why do memcpy and memmove differ?

hints.1: Ask what each keyword prevents: compiler elision versus torn updates across cores.
hints.2: Split audience: hardware/ISR vs threads; then split copy APIs by overlap permission.
hints.3: volatile ≠ atomic/barrier; threads need _Atomic or mutexes; memcpy's restrict enables faster non-overlap copies, memmove allows overlap.

phases.goal: Apply qualifiers to real sites: MMIO, ISRs/signals, polling loops, and const-correct APIs.

must_hit.point: volatile is required for memory-mapped hardware registers, globals modified by an ISR, and sig_atomic_t variables modified in a signal handler.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists MMIO, ISR-shared globals, and volatile sig_atomic_t for signal handlers.

must_hit.point: Without volatile, a polling loop on a flag the compiler thinks is unchanged can hoist the load and become an infinite loop; with volatile, each iteration emits a fresh load so hardware updates are observed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Traces non-volatile wait loop optimized to if (flag==0) while(1); versus per-iteration loads with volatile.

must_hit.point: Passing overlapping buffers to memcpy breaks the restrict promise and is undefined behavior; the compiler may have vectorized assuming no overlap, causing corruption.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States overlapping memcpy is UB due to broken restrict, unlike memmove.

probes: Walk through a hardware-flag polling loop with and without volatile, and say when you would mark a pointer const volatile.

hints.1: Imagine something outside the C abstract machine changing a location between your statements.
hints.2: Consider optimizer hoisting of loop loads, then MMIO/ISR/signal cases, then restrict lies.
hints.3: Non-volatile flag can become if (0) infinite spin; volatile reloads each time; const volatile fits read-only async hardware registers; overlapping memcpy is UB.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: volatile ensures compiler-visible memory accesses for hardware and ISRs but gives neither atomicity nor a CPU memory barrier; _Atomic (C11) gives atomicity and ordering for thread communication—use volatile for hardware/interrupts, _Atomic or mutexes for OS threads.
memcpy promises non-overlapping dest/src via restrict and can use aggressive vectorization; memmove makes no restrict promise, correctly handles overlap, and may be slower.

tradeoffs.topic: const vs volatile on hardware registers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: const alone would allow caching of a value that hardware still changes; volatile alone would allow the program to write a read-only register; const volatile forces fresh reads while forbidding C-side writes.

gotchas.trap: Casting away const and modifying an object that was originally defined as const (e.g. string literal or const global).
gotchas.correction: That is undefined behavior; the object may live in read-only memory (.rodata) and the OS may segfault on the write.

gotchas.trap: Using volatile for inter-thread synchronization (the concurrency myth).
gotchas.correction: volatile is not atomic and not a memory barrier; it does not stop data races or CPU reordering—use _Atomic or mutexes.

gotchas.trap: Passing overlapping buffers to memcpy because it “just copies memory.”
gotchas.correction: That breaks the restrict promise and is undefined behavior; use memmove when overlap is possible.

gotchas.trap: Omitting volatile on a flag polled in a tight loop that hardware or an ISR updates.
gotchas.correction: The optimizer may hoist the read and turn the wait into an infinite loop that never observes the update.
